items.title: Japanese Indie Gaming Publishers Are Doing Things Differently
items.author: Alicia Haddick
items.summary: Tokyo Game Show 2026 was light on major upcoming releases, in part due to a quieter-than-normal fall for gaming outside of the unavoidable spectre of Grand
items.text:
Tokyo Game Show 2026 was light on major upcoming releases, in part due to a quieter-than-normal fall for gaming outside of the unavoidable spectre of Grand Theft Auto VI. That being said, there were still things to see at this year’s event—you just had to know where to look. Take a glance at the world of Japanese indie gaming showcased on the convention floor, for example, and you would find a wonderful assortment of unique experiences rooted in Japanese social issues and experiences, the results of a notable divergence from how Japanese indie games have historically been developed, supported, and shared with players.

It may be somewhat surprising that it’s taken until the last few years for a groundswell of Japanese indie developers to establish themselves within the domestic games industry. Indie gaming has thrived since the late 2000s outside of Japan thanks to digital storefronts on consoles, and Japan itself is host to events like Comiket, where both amateur original and derivative works in various art forms, including video games, can be sold. These works are known as doujin.

At their core, doujin games were acts of love created by hobbyist developers to sell to core fans, whether original or derivative of another IP. The Touhou franchise, arguably the biggest example of Japanese independent gaming media in the past 30 years, rose from this subculture. Otherwise, however, doujin has been mostly a passion-fueled endeavor, a way to share creations with like-minded fans more than a path to profit or a potential career.

Yet as global indie darlings like Undertale, sustained marketing efforts like Nintendo’s Indie World, and Japanese indie companies like Q-Games and Orbitals developer Shapefarm find success, some have felt encouraged to break from the norm of major company employment and challenge themselves to give indie game development a shot. With more teams and creators embracing this field, the results are often unique experiences that channel Japanese societal practices and personal experiences.

Mask It, featured at Tokyo Game Show this year as part of the Selected Indie 80, a program designed to bring attention to standout indie efforts, began as a Game Jam project during this year’s Global Game Jam. Players assume the role of a news editor whose job is to make the everyday news more “exciting” to hit targets and please editors, often by deliberately blurring over photographs or making other edits in stories as you seek sensationalistic virality. These tweaks could merely be done for comedic effect, or to insinuate sinister implications and have a corrosive impact on public discourse or opinion, making the game a reflection of increasing concerns in Japan over the spread of false information on social media and by politicians, alongside concerns about AI.

Timemoon, from developer Kenkou Land, is a narrative adventure in which you play as Clark, a taxi driver in the near future taking passengers in his time-traveling taxi. A passenger’s destination may not just be a location but a moment in time, and following the mysterious death of the president, your chauffeuring of high-profile passengers may be key to understanding the possible use of time travel in their murder.

Then you have Late Fee Girls, an RPG following three girls who run a video store and make secondary revenue as Exorcist Streamers, going out to fight ghosts from haunted videotapes. It’s an ambitious project for solo developer Urimo, who is concurrently selling doujin comics that contain character sketches and in-universe commentary from the characters as development continues.

There were plenty of other exciting indie games at TGS this year, too, like Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, which features a bicycling tanuki running errands and pulling tricks like Tony Hawk, and Iron Bramble, a Metroidvania with a unique grappling hook–driven movement system. But it’s the doujin magazines of Late Fee Girls that reveal, on a more intimate scale, how Japanese doujin and indie game creators are finding different pathways toward funding development, building audiences, and sustaining their work.

Developers like them are increasingly embracing the ecosystems in place for small creators to sell their creations and showcase their work at everything from vast conventions to minor art gallery spaces as a way to fund game development. Selling stickers or postcards or a small zine of concept art may not make a huge dent in development budgets, but it helps by also leaving the people who buy them invested in the game as they wait for the release and spread the word.

And these events, even those that aren’t gaming-specific, can draw thousands of eyes to your game. Some will sell doujins even at more generalized events like Comitia, whose quarterly Tokyo events attract over 30,000 attendees each, while Comiket can attract over 300,000 people over its two days.

This strategy of selling merchandise for in-development and post-release games while also looking toward multimedia expansion to make an impression and grow an IP’s audience was the founding principle of a number of Japan-centric publishers showcasing at this year’s TGS.

The winner of the best indie game at Tokyo Game Show, taking away the Platinum Prize for best game as part of the event’s Selected Indie 80, was Finding Polka, a beautiful game about searching for a missing dog in a dense town, with a visual style defined by hand-drawn sketches for every character and animation. Also taking away top prizes at Gamescom and Japanese indie gaming event Bitsummit, the game is published by Parco Games worldwide, a new games publisher founded by the Japanese department store chain of the same name.

The company’s large department stores across Japan are home to far more than just clothing, with Parco investing heavily in everything from art exhibitions to stage plays. Parco Games is also forming partnerships outside of publishing, like a pop-up store for Kojima Productions, and its efforts with indie developers extend to merchandising.

Thus, you can buy Finding Polka t-shirts from Parco, sold alongside major fashion brands online, and the company is embracing an arts-driven approach to the games it partners with. Finding Polka is one of the first titles it’s publishing globally, but the company is also working with Turkish team Error Thing to publish Deperson worldwide, a highlight of the show for its unnerving creativity. This psychedelic horror game set inside a mental hospital features alluring hand-drawn art as you speak with other patients, learning about their conditions and dealing with amnesia. While not a Japanese game, Parco’s interest in artistic expression made partnering with it a natural fit, according to the Parco Games team.

“We aren’t a game-centric company, but we have a long history of discovering new talent and innovative forms of expression, and bringing their appeal to a wide audience,” explains Yudai Kawamura from Parco Games. “We believe our experience here can be applied to the world of gaming as well. Parco has physical spaces where people can gather such as stores, event spaces, galleries and theaters, and allowing people to experience games not just by selling them but through exhibitions and events is something unique to what we offer.”

The company’s hope is that emphasizing a game as a long-term piece of art beyond just the video-game space will help it to resonate. And this approach doesn’t stop with Parco Games. In recent years, Shueisha Games has used its parent company’s experience as a manga publisher to assist in expanding its successful games into new mediums like novels and pop-up merchandising stores in physical retail locations.

Beyond simply being great games by a breadth of developers from a range of backgrounds, these games all feature original ideas and are being supported by publishers for whom gaming is just one avenue to promote the developers they work with. It elevates games to the level of an exhibition in an art gallery, and a conversation piece that can linger beyond the next refresh of a digital storefront, creating an environment in which it’s easier to take a risk on a new idea.

Currently, the Japanese indie games able to break out internationally are viral phenomena like Meccha Chamelion and Exit 8, but it’s titles like Finding Polka that showcase a creative indie scene that can sustain itself, and that invites global players to explore what it holds. Japanese indie gaming was thriving at Tokyo Game Show, because it chose to do things differently.

items.title: Phantom Blade Zero’s Fast-Paced Action Took 15 Years, Two RPG-Maker Games, And A Whole Lot Of Money To Bring To Life
items.author: Lex Luddy

items.text:
I’ve been tracking the release of Phantom Blade Zero for several years now, playing the game multiple times over the course of three years, from demos that felt like little more than vertical slices all the way to a multi-hour hands-on at Gamescom this year. For a time, it felt like the game had come out of nowhere; I’d never encountered Chinese developer S-Game’s previous titles, and assumed they were never released outside of the country. However, it turns out I simply wasn’t paying attention, and Phantom Blade Zero is part of a franchise known as Rainblood that’s over 15 years old and features a longtime series protagonist who has only so many days to live, while the games themselves have sought to create their own new genre and style.

These titles are turn-based RPGs set in the same world as Phantom Blade, and seem to share almost no gameplay DNA with the upcoming triple-A game. In 2013, they were followed up by Rain Blood Chronicles: Mirage (yes, Rain Blood is two words now), a Unity-powered hack-and-slash 2D brawler which did actually make its way to Steam and consoles—though the Xbox and PlayStation versions now seem to be delisted.

All three of these games are noticeably unpolished, but make up for it with their striking, dark and twisted interpretation of the Ming Dynasty. Following Mirage, S-game published three China-exclusive mobile games. Then in May 2023, Phantom Blade Zero, a big-budget 3D action game, was announced, followed by the release of Phantom Blade: Executioners in November, a 2D beat ’em up which came out on PS4, PS5, and mobile, though again the console ports seem to have been pulled. Both of these games share commonalities with Soulframe’s earlier releases, most notably a recurring motif of crimson blades wielded by the protagonist that stand out in the often grim and grey world; however, these games feel noticeably small compared to a triple-A game featuring Donnie Yen.

All this leads to the question: Where did the exponential increase in fidelity and scope come from? While the second of these projects, “Stellar Saga,” is still MIA, the other is the continuation of Soulframe’s long-running series. Which all brings us to now, and my four-ish hours with Phantom Blade Zero.

Something that I have noted in my previous time with this game is that while it bears some surface-level similarities to the assortment of Chinese-developed Souls-inspired games like Black Myth: Wukong and Wuchang: Fallen Feathers, in practice it plays closer to a hybrid of Sekiro and Devil May Cry, fusing elements of the former’s fast, stagger-focused combat with the latter’s stylish action-game sensibilities.

This design ethos is best showcased in how the stamina bar functions. Oftentimes in games that seek to offer a faster version of a typical Souls-like combat system, I find myself frustrated by the fact that I can combo chains of attacks with flashy animations, but because each swing of the sword eats away at my stamina bar, I often find myself incapable of extricating myself from enemies’ ripostes. Phantom Blade addresses this, as your stamina doesn’t go down when attacking or successfully blocking, only when dodging or attempting to block certain color-coded attacks. Moreover, your light attacks do not take animation priority over all other inputs, meaning that if you start a swing only to realize a boss will strike you first, you can quickly hit block mid-attack to protect yourself.

This focus on offensive combat over a muddled mix of Souls-ish turtling, stamina regen, and protracted combos instantly makes Phantom Blade both more intuitive than some of its closest contemporaries and more compelling and cohesive. The design seems to be less focused on finding ways to force wuxia into a Souls game and more focused on creating a combat system purpose-built to highlight both the flow and speed of wuxia media, resulting in something I find infinitely more interesting and rewarding.

Phantom Blade’s free-flowing combat focuses on 30 primary weapons, each with its own unique moveset and properties, and 25 secondary weapons, some of which, like axes, grant you heavy charge attacks while others, like mini-cannons, are slow-firing ranged weapons. You can equip two primary weapons at a time, keeping one off-hand and ready to go; however, while you can simply swap to your other primary by hitting the D-pad, you can also work it into a combo with the left trigger. This system is interesting because the combo-weapon-change both deal a lot of damage and stagger to enemies but is also on a cooldown, meaning that if you get into a good flow dealing with a boss with a longsword, comboing away from it to your dual-blades might not actually be the best move.

While the combat of Phantom Blade Zero feels distinctly un-Soulslike, the same cannot be said for the world. The press release for the game highlights that Phantom Blade’s interconnected world is “inspired by Soulslike map design.” In lieu of a traditional, highly detailed video game map, you’re instead provided with hand-painted, ink wash–style charts of the area painted on Xuan paper and scanned into the game. This more abstract map is paired with level design that often doubles back and reconnects to other areas in a way most reminiscent of the first Dark Souls game.

It’s not surprising that S-Game acknowledges FromSoftware’s genre-defining franchise in official press materials, because its fingerprints are everywhere in the world design. Beyond just the interconnected map, Phantom Blade’s version of the Ming Dynasty is a world of decay and plague that feels very much at home in the video game pantheon of “mysterious, doomed and cursed worlds inspired by Demon’s Souls.” While at times environments can look washed-out, it feels like a conscious design decision that highlights the decline of this warring region. Flashes of steampunk industrialization give Phantom Blade an additional bit of life and serve as an interesting way to diversify the visuals. It also gives S-game plenty of room to showcase monstrous enemies that are grotesque due to inhumane and ramshackle mechanized corruption instead of the genre-standard mystic rot that sometimes feels overdone.

Bosses demand the kind of pattern recognition typical of Soulslike bosses over the fast reaction speed you might be used to from a Ninja Gaiden or DMC. There’s still plenty of blocking, parrying, and clashing of swords to build stagger, but these encounters require that you outright avoid certain attacks over simply finding ways to deal with them. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but I did find myself enjoying the frenetic push-forward nature of encounters with groups of standard enemies over the more considered pacing of bosses. Dealing with bosses’ relentless, unblockable attacks that force you to focus on positioning over fast reactions feels like a strange deviation for a combat system designed to reward getting up in enemies’ faces.

While I was generally sold on nearly everything Phantom Blade Zero presented—the world is interesting, the combat is fun and layered—I did find the story comparably dry. The game’s protagonist, Soul, is featured in all three Rainblood games, and the new release seemingly retells certain parts of them. In the first Rainblood, Soul also had a limited number of days to live, having had his heart pierced by a cursed blade, which either means that Phantom Blade Zero retells parts of Town of Death, or Soul has a chronic cardiac penetration problem.

On three of the game’s difficulties, this countdown is purely narrative; however, you can opt to play on an extra-hard mode which ties this plot point into the gameplay, counting down a day each time Soul dies in battle. This ticking clock is pretty much the only part of the otherwise pretty standard revenge plot that hooked me, and hearing that it’s been relegated to a difficulty setting most players will probably avoid kind of strips it of most of its stakes. While there is some level of intrigue generated by Soul’s limited time to live, the rest of the characters that I encountered during my time with Phantom Blade were far less compelling, opting mostly to espouse platitudes on darkness, personal codes, and vague ideals.

The only real standout in the cast is Mó Yuan, portrayed by Donnie Yen. The star of the upcoming John Wick spin-off Caine, Yen also apparently consulted on the game’s action alongside stuntman and choreographer Kenji Tanigaki. While I love plenty of Yen’s action movies, the casting of the martial arts superstar does little to flesh out the experience beyond a brief moment of me going “oh, that guy” when he shows up.

Phantom Blade Zero fascinates me. The sheer escalation in scale from Soulframe and S-Game’s earlier works is hard to overstate, and while it’s tempting to get out there early and celebrate something like that, polish, bombast, and scope don’t always equate to quality. After my most recent hands-on with Phantom Blade, I’ve found myself going back to the RPG-maker footage of the original Rainblood. It’s a somewhat scruffy passion project, with a near-endless supply of charm and grit. Phantom Blade Zero is plenty promising; however, it feels like some amount of that original game’s soul may have been lost in translation over the 15-year journey and the hundreds of millions of dollars. As it stands now, while I remain interested in yet another big-budget action game coming out of China, I think I am going to go track down one of those fan sites and start a playthrough of a Chinese turn-based RPG from 2011, because Town of Death seems cool as hell.

items.text:
To say that the AI boom has caused a certain level of existential dread is not an understatement, mainly because it’s being spearheaded and controlled by a chosen few without much regulation (for now). It’s become a hot button topic, and Cupertino thankfully isn’t subtle about which side it’s on. In the opening seconds of Robert and Michelle King‘s’ legal dramedy, attorney Michael Price (Mike Colter) packs up his desk after he’s fired from a tech startup that he invested in. The first item in his filing box? A chocolate bar named David. At episode’s end, Michael states that the mission of his brand new law firm—which he launches alongside lawyer Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller)—is akin to the David vs. Goliath saga. That is, they’re the heroic underdogs facing off against powerful Silicon Valley companies. They’ll only take on clients no one else will out of fear of pissing off the Goliaths. With that, Cupertino sets up its resonant premise: It will examine tech’s unavoidable encroachment into our lives, and its extremely harmful influence.


It all starts with, as the episode’s title suggests, “Michael And Olivia.” The two are let go from the successful S-Talk on the same day for different, shady reasons. Michael is falsely accused of proprietary leaks so his co-founder, Richard Everett (Will Brill), can keep Michael’s equity; Olivia is fired before she can tell anyone Richard sexually harassed her by sending her a dick pic. Wrongfully terminated by and angry at their employer, Michael and Olivia team up to bring two lawsuits against S-Talk. However, Olivia is resistant at first, knowing that her traditional family wouldn’t want her to make public such a private matter. It’s not until she finds out that Richard modeled Daisy—his next-level generative AI model—after her that Olivia decides to fight back.


Cupertino gives Olivia a lot of layers right away: She’s a religious conservative who prays often and keeps a Bible at her desk; she’s also open-minded and couldn’t wait to leave her Wisconsin hometown after graduation; she’s soft-spoken and therefore frequently underestimated. The Kings infuse her with a lot of personality, including her love of musicals. (She hums Annie‘s “It’s A Hard Knock Life” whenever she’s nervous, which is the kind of character detail that quickly helps the audience understand her.) Best known for her work in grittier dramas like Legion, Tokyo Vice, and The Society, Keller brings an admirable tenderness to the character. Colter matches her performance, mixing Michael’s swagger with vulnerability. The Evil actor straddles Michael’s professional ambitions, family pressures, and morality.


Unlike his wealthy celebrity lawyer father, Bayard (Joe Morton)—who drops in just to chastise his son—Michael doesn’t want to represent bigwigs. Instead, he hopes to stand for those wronged by Big Tech heavyweights. So he encourages Olivia to do the same without being pushy or demanding. Michael and Olivia end up getting along swimmingly, working out their respective lawsuits from an IHOP until Michael’s spunky, resourceful assistant helps them out. Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller)—also fired from S-Talk—joins the two lawyers, using her blue-collar family’s contacts to secure them a lavish workspace. Or rather, a fancy reception area, because the actual cubicles inside the building don’t exist yet. Once the firm starts making money, the plan is to build one room after another. Until then, the chic lobby will have to do.


Once “Michael And Olivia” heads to court, Richard’s lawyer (played by Steven Pasquale) gives them a hard time. Still, Michael and Olivia put up a solid fight. Most of the argument boils down to Richard’s mortifying new gen-AI creation, Daisy, whose voice and “personality” are freakishly similar to that of Olivia, who clarifies that she trained Daisy as part of an assignment; she didn’t know Richard was essentially cloning her. All of this derails S-Talk’s 14-day deadline to raise funds, especially since Olivia also points out that the company’s biggest VC donor has spoken out against DEI (so it looks worse that their only Black lawyer was fired).


At the end of all this, Richard and Ry end up offering a whole lot of money in a settlement deal. We don’t see the exact number, but it’s enough for Michael, Olivia, and Christy to celebrate that they can now officially kick off this law firm and start seeking clients. Just as Michael and Olivia jot down and sign their 50-50 partnership on a pillar, the elevator dings and in walks a bewildered new client (played by Nik Dodani) desperately seeking their help.


As far as series premieres go, Cupertino is both exciting and essential. Directed by Robert King and co-written by the husband-wife duo, it succeeds at not only introducing and fleshing out the world and those who populate it, but most importantly, puts forth the show’s vision in a crystal clear way. Michael and Olivia might have lost the battle (the judge did side with Richard in Olivia’s lawsuit, and Michael’s was settled out of court), but Cupertino is sure shaping them to win the war.


Stray observations:

• Debra Monk and David Aaron Baker guest star as Olivia’s parents, who rush to California to bring their daughter home after she’s fired and appear skeptical of her partnership with Michael.


• There’s a funny running gag throughout this episode wherein the strangers Michael meets (his cab driver, the process server, etc.) pitch him ideas for their shopping, catering, and ride share startups.


• The fledgling firm hires actors to fool Richard and Ry into thinking it’s already successful and potentially backed by Bayard. Good thinking!


• Once Michael finds out Olivia has a thing for musicals, he sends her a playlist so she can listen to “real music,” and it’s composed of songs by Fantastic Negrito.


• Try not to feel total and complete terror at the following defense that Ry gives for S-Talk in court about their AI principles in an effort to prove that Daisy isn’t based on Olivia: “We train from everyone’s personalities online. Millions of people from Reddit, X, Meta, from novels, articles, and on Zoom. It’s the grand melting pot of AI. It’s called fair use.”

Saloni Gajjar is The A.V. Club‘s TV critic.

Directed by Robert King and co-written by the husband-wife duo, it succeeds at not only introducing and fleshing out the world and those who populate it, but most importantly, puts forth the show’s vision in a crystal clear way. Michael and Olivia might have lost the battle (the judge did side with Richard in Olivia’s lawsuit, and Michael’s was settled out of court), but Cupertino is sure shaping them to win the war.
Stray observations:
• Debra Monk and David Aaron Baker guest star as Olivia’s parents, who rush to California to bring their daughter home after she’s fired and appear skeptical of her partnership with Michael.

• There’s a funny running gag throughout this episode wherein the strangers Michael meets (his cab driver, the process server, etc.) pitch him ideas for their shopping, catering, and ride share startups.
• The fledgling firm hires actors to fool Richard and Ry into thinking it’s already successful and potentially backed by Bayard. Good thinking!
• Once Michael finds out Olivia has a thing for musicals, he sends her a playlist so she can listen to “real music,” and it’s composed of songs by Fantastic Negrito.

• Try not to feel total and complete terror at the following defense that Ry gives for S-Talk in court about their AI principles in an effort to prove that Daisy isn’t based on Olivia: “We train from everyone’s personalities online. Millions of people from Reddit, X, Meta, from novels, articles, and on Zoom. It’s the grand melting pot of AI. It’s called fair use.”
Saloni Gajjar is The A.V. Club‘s TV critic.

items.text:
Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg (“The Social Reckoning”), Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (“You Can See Everything”), Elon Musk (Alex Gibney’s “Musk”), and OpenAI’s Sam Altman (“Artificial”). Television is in on the trend, too. In November, Netflix will remind us of the implosion of cryptocurrency fund FTX and its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, in “The Altruists.”

On CBS and Paramount+ starting Thursday, there’s “Cupertino,” a broadcast-network procedural that doesn’t zero in on a real-life tech bro, but does raise a lot of sobering questions about the industry currently attempting to cram A.I. down the throats of the global populace.

Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

“I’m sick of people controlling my fate, and my guess is there are a lot of people out there that feel the same way but don’t have anyone to represent them,” says Michael Price (Mike Colter of “Luke Cage” and “Evil”), an attorney who co-founded, then got edged out of, an extremely successful big tech company called S-Talk.

He’s explaining his reasons for wanting to start an agency that takes on the cases against Magnificent 7-level companies that other firms are too afraid to touch. But he could just as easily be describing this show’s appeal to an American audience frustrated by the unemployment rate, the disproportionate power and wealth of the billionaire class, and the non-stop insistence that everyone get on board with artificial intelligence.

Unlike the other projects mentioned above, “Cupertino” does not focus on the idiosyncrasies/neuroses of a single, perceived “genius.” It is more general in its depiction of big tech, which enables it to feel both timely and, perhaps, more relatable to the average person.

Pictured (L-R): Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre and Mike Colter as Michael Price. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved.

While there are some key storylines that run throughout the first 10 episodes—the rivalry between Michael and his showboating lawyer father (Joe Morton); another, separate rivalry between Michael and his ex, also an attorney (Renée Elise Goldsberry, who co-starred opposite Colter on “Evil”); and, most importantly, an ongoing narrative about a particularly dangerous form of AI—this is largely a case-of-the-week type of show.

With its quick, plot-driven pacing, “Cupertino” is episodic, mainstream network storytelling that shows, like so much of the Kings’ output, that it’s still possible to make smart, sophisticated, digestible television within that framework.

As Michael, Colter is dignified, pragmatic and, if I’m being honest, not wildly different in demeanor from David, the priest the actor played on “Evil.” But he’s a persuasive lead in both shows, so I’m not going to complain too much about any overlap. While Michael believes in justice and the rule of law, he’s not some anti-capitalist hero who wants to burn down all of Silicon Valley. He simply sees a gap in the marketplace that needs filling. “When you’re in the middle of the ocean, you don’t sell people more water,” he explains to Goldsberry’s Nichole. “You sell them life jackets.”

His partner at the new firm, Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), a devout Christian and gifted lawyer who also gets fired from S-Talk after being sexually harassed by the head of the company, is the bleeding heart in this pairing. Keller and Colter have an organic, friendly chemistry that, to the show’s credit, is supportive without being romantic, at least not in these early episodes.

But the standout performances in “Cupertino” come from the two actors who provide the most comedic relief in a drama that doesn’t shy away from poking fun at the always-pitching culture of venture capitalism. Ella Stiller (daughter of Ben Stiller and Christine Taylor) gets a break-out role as Christy Palladino, a third employee who gets fired from S-Talk and becomes the receptionist at Price and Siffre, where she proves to be a fantastic investigator for her attorney bosses.

Christy is particularly adept at tracking down leads and calling in favors from her extensive family of blue-collar workers; after being escorted out of the S-Talk building, she phones her electrician uncle, who proceeds to turn the power on and off in that office and enrage everyone still “lucky” enough to be employed there. Christy knows nothing about technology, but she loves to stick it to the man. Her default expression is resting “you’ve got to be kidding me” face, and Stiller has got that expression down pat.

Pictured (L-R): Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved

Then there’s Busy Phillips, who’s cast as Natalia Boutella, a key investor in the new firm who also happens to be divorced from a tech executive played by Fisher Stevens who is not Jeff Bezos, but also is totally Jeff Bezos. Natalia is less interested in sticking it to the man than she is in sticking it to that particular man. When he denies that he has gained weight after she tells him he “got fat,” Natalia counters: “You dined with the president, you had a front row seat to that inauguration, you bought a billion-dollar yacht. You got fat.” Phillips utters lines like that as if they’re coated in venom.

(As an added bonus, every time she and Goldsberry appear in the same scene, it’s like a partial “Girls5Eva” reunion, and that alone deserves a fresh designation on Rotten Tomatoes.)

The Kings and co. tackle numerous zeitgeisty tech trends; one episode focuses on a teenager compelled to kill his father by a chatbot, while another, which happens to debut less than a week before the midterms, zeroes in on prediction websites used to manipulate elections.

But “Cupertino” is not a purely anti-A.I. narrative. The episodes also highlight situations where technological assistance can help. In one, Christy gets incredibly frustrated by an A.I. agent she attempts to train by making sure its knowledge of horror movies is up to snuff. (“In which state did ‘The Blair Witch Project‘ take place?” she asks. “Wisconsin,” the agent cheerfully responds. Christy: “No, Maryland, moron.”) But she’s pretty grateful for that moron when he can warn her not to take a sip of a drink that’s been spiked at a bar.

If “Cupertino” has an official position on technology, it’s that it can be very useful, but it desperately needs significant, legally enforceable guardrails. This is an opinion shared by most sentient beings with anything akin to a conscience. This series dares to suggest that there’s a world where guardrails could be put in place, and where the “little guys” in the tech world have a chance to be heard. Maybe that’s a fantasy, but it’s one that’s extremely entertaining to live in for 42 minutes every week.

The first ten episodes of season one were screened in advance for critics. An additional ten episodes are currently in production.

With Mike Flanagan’s series adaptation arriving on streaming this week, Stephen King’s Carrie is once again at the top of every horror fan’s mind. The debut novel of the King of Horror, Carrie is a highly influential teen horror book that follows a friendless girl from an abusive home who discovers latent psychic abilities. In the aftermath of a cruel prank, she unleashes these powers on all the people who have made her life hell. Though it wasn’t an instant success when it first hit the shelves in 1974, the book went on to become a critical and fan favorite, launching King’s spectacularly successful career as a master of the horror genre.

Between its literary success and the multiple adaptations it has inspired, Carrie is easily one of the most iconic horror novels of the 20th century. And as an iconic novel, it has inspired several subsequent works that have expanded on its premise and themes in fascinating ways. Beyond those it inspired, the legendary coming-of-age horror story has also been compared over the years to a number of books with similar themes, including some by King himself. So, without further ado, here’s our handpicked list of horror books that we think you should have on your reading list if you’re a fan of Carrie.

1
‘The Long Walk’ (1979)

Image via Signet Books

Written by Stephen King and published under the pseudonym Richard Bachman, The Long Walk is a dystopian novel set in a totalitarian USA, centered on the titular annual walking contest, in which 100 boys are forced to continuously walk at a pace of four miles per hour until all but one is dead. The survivor is promised their heart’s desire, but the chances of survival are less than slim. The novel centers on Ray Garraty, one of the contestants, and explores his experiences and those of his fellow contestants.

An exceptionally bleak teen dystopia, The Long Walk is technically the first book King wrote, though Carrie was his first novel to be published. It’s a powerful story that predates the early 21st-century rise in YA dystopias and delivers a grueling yet touching experience, exploring themes of mortality, humanity, and the psychological toll of totalitarianism. The novel got its first film adaptation in 2025, over 40 years after it was first published, with Francis Lawrence directing and Cooper Hoffman starring as Ray.

2
‘The Weight of Blood’ (2022)

Image via HarperCollins Publishers

A 21st-century retelling of Carrie, The Weight of Blood is a young adult horror novel written by Tiffany D. Jackson. The narrative alternates between a present-day podcast exploring the case of a massive fire at a prom in the small Georgia town of Springville, and 2014, when the events actually took place. At the center of the story is biracial high school senior Maddy Washington. Forced to pass as white by her racist father and bullied by her classmates, Maddy discovers her innate telekinetic abilities and unleashes them on the unsuspecting town after being humiliated during prom night.

The Weight of Blood is essentially a loose remake of Carrie, using the same basic storyline and epistolary structure to explore more contemporary themes and perspectives. A story of racism, identity, and empowerment, the novel is faithful to the core of King’s original work while delivering a distinct message and reading experience. The novel earned critical acclaim at the time of its publication in 2022 and was nominated for a Bram Stoker Award; it’s an easy recommendation for any fan of Carrie, particularly if you’re interested in seeing the story expanded upon in a more contemporary context, like in Flanagan's series adaptation.

3
‘Mary: An Awakening of Terror’ (2022)

Image via Tor Nightfire

Nat Cassidy’s Mary: An Awakening of Terror is a horror novel that follows a woman’s supernatural awakening, but unlike Carrie, Mary is a quiet, middle-aged woman grappling with the physical and psychological toll of perimenopause. Unfortunately, along with the hot flashes and body aches, she’s also been hearing voices and experiencing terrifying visions. And to make things worse, she discovers that her strange experiences may be connected to an infamous serial killer.

Often compared to Carrie by horror fans, Mary: An Awakening of Terror is a gripping work of psychological and supernatural horror. Its similarities to Carrie, however, are only surface-level, as the story progresses into a dark conspiracy involving a shadowy cult and a secret history of violence. At the time of its release in 2022, the novel was hailed as one of the best books of the year by Esquire, CrimeReads, and more, and though it’s relatively underrated, the book has proven quite popular in genre circles. It’s a great read, especially for the Halloween season, with visceral horrors and a dark sense of humor.

What Is Your Biggest Horror Nightmare?
Elm Street · Chucky · Scream · The Conjuring

Four horror franchises. Four completely different ways of scaring you. One waits until you fall asleep. One makes sure nobody believes you. One is already in your group of friends. And one is in the house with your family. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually watch horror, and find out which nightmare was built for you.

🧸Chucky(Child's Play)

📞Scream(Ghostface)

🕯️The Conjuring(The Warren Files)

FIND YOUR NIGHTMARE →

01

Which horror scene makes you cover your eyes?
Four classic images. One of them is worse than the others for you.

ASomebody falling asleep when they really should not.
BA toy that has moved, and nobody touched it.
CA phone ringing in an empty house.
DA child talking to somebody who is not there.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

You are home alone and you hear a noise. First thought?
Everybody has one. It arrives before you have decided anything.

AI am exhausted and my mind is playing tricks on me.
BSomething in this room is not where I left it.
CSomebody is in here with me.
DThis house has never felt entirely right.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Which horror movie rule would you break first?
Everybody thinks they would survive. Almost nobody actually does.

ANever fall asleep.
BNever leave it out of your sight.
CNever answer the phone.
DNever go down to the basement.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Something genuinely frightening happens. What do you do?
Not in a film. In your actual living room, tonight.

AConvince myself I imagined the whole thing.
BTell someone, and brace for them not believing me.
CWork out which person I know could be behind it.
DGet everybody in the house into one room.

Be honest about this one. Nobody is checking.

AFine during. Wide awake at two in the morning.

NEXT QUESTION →

Somebody offers you serious money. Which do you still refuse?
The amount does not matter. There is one on this list you are not doing.

AFall asleep in a room I have never been in before.
BKeep an old doll on the shelf facing my bed.
CAnswer every unknown number that calls after midnight.

NEXT QUESTION →

Which feeling stays with you a week after the film?

ANot wanting to turn the bedroom light off.

NEXT QUESTION →

Something wakes you at 3am. What is the worst possibility?

AThat I am still asleep, and it knows it.
BThat the thing nobody believed me about is here.
CThat somebody with a key is downstairs.
DThat something is in the doorway, watching us sleep.

REVEAL MY NIGHTMARE →

The Lights Just Went Out
Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.

A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984

Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.

You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.

Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988

Chucky

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.

By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.

Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996

Scream

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.

Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.

The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013

The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

4
‘The Power’ (2016)

Image via Viking

Written by Naomi Alderman, The Power is a sci-fi novel that explores an alternate timeline in which women around the world develop the ability to release electric jolts from their fingers. The story is presented as a nested narrative, following a manuscript about 21st-century history that’s submitted to the author for an early read, set 5,000 years in our relative future. A key event within this imagined history is a Cataclysm, in which one of the newly empowered women destroys all modern technology, with the novel exploring the events that led up to this disastrous incident.

Published in 2016, The Power was fairly well-received by critics and contemporary authors, earning praise for its feminist themes. While the novel’s narrative can be a bit uneven in parts, its execution is highly engaging, and it’s ultimately a thrilling read. The book uses the reversal of gender norms to deliver some keen observations on human sociology and psychology that extend beyond its surface-level apocalypse. A series adaptation developed by Alderman, Raelle Tucker, Claire Wilson, and Sarah Quintrell was released on Prime Video in 2023, with Toni Collette, Halle Bush, Auliʻi Cravalho, and more starring in key roles.

5
‘Witchcraft for Wayward Girls’ (2025)

Image via Penguin Random House

Written by Grady Hendrix, Witchcraft for Wayward Girls is a period folk horror novel set in 1970s Florida. The book revolves around a group of pregnant teenagers who are sent to an abusive maternity home. When they discover a book on witchcraft, it sets the girls on a path of revenge and dark magic where the hope of liberation is tempered by the sinister cost of consorting with witches.

Released in 2025, Witchcraft for Wayward Girls has earned a generally favorable reception from critics and horror fans. While the book may not be quite as scary as Hendrix’s previous bestsellers, it retains the author’s dark sense of humor, which is used very effectively to balance the novel’s true horrors: the real-life maternity homes that inspired the story and the abuses they inflict upon these young girls. More than the actual supernatural elements, it’s these realities that make Witchcraft for Wayward Girls so very horrifying and lead to its most heartbreaking moments. It’s easily one of the best horror novels of the past year, and a must-read for fans of Carrie and The Craft.

6
‘The Merciless’ (2014)

Image via Penguin Random House

Danielle Vega’s debut novel, The Merciless, is the first book in the Young Adult novel series. The book follows teenager Sofia Flores, a military brat who arrives in a new town and befriends a trio of popular girls. When her new friends rope her in on a plan to kidnap local goth Brooklyn and perform an exorcism on her, Sofia faces a twisted choice between allowing the torture to continue or saving the girl while risking herself.

As the title suggests, The Merciless is full of intense horror and suspense, with torture scenes that are not for the weak-stomached. Though it's often compared to the teen comedy Mean Girls, The Merciless uses the same basic premise to launch a tense horror story that goes to some pretty disturbing places, particularly once the true nature of the story is revealed by its shocking twist. It might not be the best YA horror book of all time, but it’s certainly one of the better ones, making it a must-read for fans of teen horror stories.

7
‘Firestarter’ (1980)

Image via Viking

Stephen King’s sci-fi horror thriller novel Firestarter explores the story of Charlie McGee, a young girl with powerful pyrokinetic abilities. The novel follows Charlie and her psychic father Andy as they go on the run, trying to evade a shadowy government agency that wants to exploit their powers for their own agenda. Hunted across the country and pushed to violence, Charlie attracts the attention of an assassin who becomes obsessed with killing her.

Both Carrie and Firestarter feature young female protagonists who possess powerful and destructive abilities, but where the former is more rooted in the coming-of-age experience, Firestarter is more of a high-tension thriller. The book quickly became a bestseller upon its publication in 1980, and it went on to win several accolades, including nominations for a British Fantasy Award and a Locus Poll Award. The novel has also inspired multiple adaptations, most famously the 1984 film directed by Mark L. Lester, which stars Drew Barrymore as Charlie, and the 2022 remake by Blumhouse Productions.

Remus is also the author of the sci-fantasy novel Once Upon a Time in Hyperspace and several works of short fiction in the mystery, comedy, and horror genres.

With Mike Flanagan’s series adaptation arriving on streaming this week, Stephen King’s Carrie is once again at the top of every horror fan’s mind. The debut novel of the King of Horror, Carrie is a highly influential teen horror book that follows a friendless girl from an abusive home who discovers latent psychic abilities. In the aftermath of a cruel prank, she unleashes these powers on all the people who have made her life hell. Though it wasn’t an instant success when it first hit the shelves in 1974, the book went on to become a critical and fan favorite, launching King’s spectacularly successful career as a master of the horror genre.

Between its literary success and the multiple adaptations it has inspired, Carrie is easily one of the most iconic horror novels of the 20th century. And as an iconic novel, it has inspired several subsequent works that have expanded on its premise and themes in fascinating ways. Beyond those it inspired, the legendary coming-of-age horror story has also been compared over the years to a number of books with similar themes, including some by King himself. So, without further ado, here’s our handpicked list of horror books that we think you should have on your reading list if you’re a fan of Carrie.

1
‘The Long Walk’ (1979)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/the-long-walk-richard-bachman.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Signet Books

Written by Stephen King and published under the pseudonym Richard Bachman, The Long Walk is a dystopian novel set in a totalitarian USA, centered on the titular annual walking contest, in which 100 boys are forced to continuously walk at a pace of four miles per hour until all but one is dead. The survivor is promised their heart’s desire, but the chances of survival are less than slim. The novel centers on Ray Garraty, one of the contestants, and explores his experiences and those of his fellow contestants.

An exceptionally bleak teen dystopia, The Long Walk is technically the first book King wrote, though Carrie was his first novel to be published. It’s a powerful story that predates the early 21st-century rise in YA dystopias and delivers a grueling yet touching experience, exploring themes of mortality, humanity, and the psychological toll of totalitarianism. The novel got its first film adaptation in 2025, over 40 years after it was first published, with Francis Lawrence directing and Cooper Hoffman starring as Ray.

2
‘The Weight of Blood’ (2022)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-25.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The Weight of Blood by Tiffany D. Jackson

blocks.x: Image via HarperCollins Publishers
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F652e35569bbcc-WhatsApp%20Image%202023-10-17%20at%2012.47.07%20PM.jpeg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

A 21st-century retelling of Carrie, The Weight of Blood is a young adult horror novel written by Tiffany D. Jackson. The narrative alternates between a present-day podcast exploring the case of a massive fire at a prom in the small Georgia town of Springville, and 2014, when the events actually took place. At the center of the story is biracial high school senior Maddy Washington. Forced to pass as white by her racist father and bullied by her classmates, Maddy discovers her innate telekinetic abilities and unleashes them on the unsuspecting town after being humiliated during prom night.

The Weight of Blood is essentially a loose remake of Carrie, using the same basic storyline and epistolary structure to explore more contemporary themes and perspectives. A story of racism, identity, and empowerment, the novel is faithful to the core of King’s original work while delivering a distinct message and reading experience. The novel earned critical acclaim at the time of its publication in 2022 and was nominated for a Bram Stoker Award; it’s an easy recommendation for any fan of Carrie, particularly if you’re interested in seeing the story expanded upon in a more contemporary context, like in Flanagan's series adaptation.

3
‘Mary: An Awakening of Terror’ (2022)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-26.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Mary: An Awakening of Terror by Nat Cassidy

blocks.x: Image via Tor Nightfire

Nat Cassidy’s Mary: An Awakening of Terror is a horror novel that follows a woman’s supernatural awakening, but unlike Carrie, Mary is a quiet, middle-aged woman grappling with the physical and psychological toll of perimenopause. Unfortunately, along with the hot flashes and body aches, she’s also been hearing voices and experiencing terrifying visions. And to make things worse, she discovers that her strange experiences may be connected to an infamous serial killer.

Often compared to Carrie by horror fans, Mary: An Awakening of Terror is a gripping work of psychological and supernatural horror. Its similarities to Carrie, however, are only surface-level, as the story progresses into a dark conspiracy involving a shadowy cult and a secret history of violence. At the time of its release in 2022, the novel was hailed as one of the best books of the year by Esquire, CrimeReads, and more, and though it’s relatively underrated, the book has proven quite popular in genre circles. It’s a great read, especially for the Halloween season, with visceral horrors and a dark sense of humor.

Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

own head is where this does its damage.

Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988

Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996
Scream

same way you watch films.

the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.

The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013
The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

4
‘The Power’ (2016)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/the-power-naomi-alderman0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The cover of the novel The Power

blocks.x: Image via Viking

Written by Naomi Alderman, The Power is a sci-fi novel that explores an alternate timeline in which women around the world develop the ability to release electric jolts from their fingers. The story is presented as a nested narrative, following a manuscript about 21st-century history that’s submitted to the author for an early read, set 5,000 years in our relative future. A key event within this imagined history is a Cataclysm, in which one of the newly empowered women destroys all modern technology, with the novel exploring the events that led up to this disastrous incident.

Published in 2016, The Power was fairly well-received by critics and contemporary authors, earning praise for its feminist themes. While the novel’s narrative can be a bit uneven in parts, its execution is highly engaging, and it’s ultimately a thrilling read. The book uses the reversal of gender norms to deliver some keen observations on human sociology and psychology that extend beyond its surface-level apocalypse. A series adaptation developed by Alderman, Raelle Tucker, Claire Wilson, and Sarah Quintrell was released on Prime Video in 2023, with Toni Collette, Halle Bush, Auliʻi Cravalho, and more starring in key roles.

5
‘Witchcraft for Wayward Girls’ (2025)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-27.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Witchcraft for Wayward Girls by Grady Hendrix

blocks.x: Image via Penguin Random House

Written by Grady Hendrix, Witchcraft for Wayward Girls is a period folk horror novel set in 1970s Florida. The book revolves around a group of pregnant teenagers who are sent to an abusive maternity home. When they discover a book on witchcraft, it sets the girls on a path of revenge and dark magic where the hope of liberation is tempered by the sinister cost of consorting with witches.

Released in 2025, Witchcraft for Wayward Girls has earned a generally favorable reception from critics and horror fans. While the book may not be quite as scary as Hendrix’s previous bestsellers, it retains the author’s dark sense of humor, which is used very effectively to balance the novel’s true horrors: the real-life maternity homes that inspired the story and the abuses they inflict upon these young girls. More than the actual supernatural elements, it’s these realities that make Witchcraft for Wayward Girls so very horrifying and lead to its most heartbreaking moments. It’s easily one of the best horror novels of the past year, and a must-read for fans of Carrie and The Craft.

6
‘The Merciless’ (2014)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-28.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Penguin Random House

Danielle Vega’s debut novel, The Merciless, is the first book in the Young Adult novel series. The book follows teenager Sofia Flores, a military brat who arrives in a new town and befriends a trio of popular girls. When her new friends rope her in on a plan to kidnap local goth Brooklyn and perform an exorcism on her, Sofia faces a twisted choice between allowing the torture to continue or saving the girl while risking herself.

As the title suggests, The Merciless is full of intense horror and suspense, with torture scenes that are not for the weak-stomached. Though it's often compared to the teen comedy Mean Girls, The Merciless uses the same basic premise to launch a tense horror story that goes to some pretty disturbing places, particularly once the true nature of the story is revealed by its shocking twist. It might not be the best YA horror book of all time, but it’s certainly one of the better ones, making it a must-read for fans of teen horror stories.

7
‘Firestarter’ (1980)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/firestarer-stephen-king.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Viking

Stephen King’s sci-fi horror thriller novel Firestarter explores the story of Charlie McGee, a young girl with powerful pyrokinetic abilities. The novel follows Charlie and her psychic father Andy as they go on the run, trying to evade a shadowy government agency that wants to exploit their powers for their own agenda. Hunted across the country and pushed to violence, Charlie attracts the attention of an assassin who becomes obsessed with killing her.

Both Carrie and Firestarter feature young female protagonists who possess powerful and destructive abilities, but where the former is more rooted in the coming-of-age experience, Firestarter is more of a high-tension thriller. The book quickly became a bestseller upon its publication in 1980, and it went on to win several accolades, including nominations for a British Fantasy Award and a Locus Poll Award. The novel has also inspired multiple adaptations, most famously the 1984 film directed by Mark L. Lester, which stars Drew Barrymore as Charlie, and the 2022 remake by Blumhouse Productions.

Nintendo Switch 2 Gamers Can Officially Grab A 10/10 RPG Completely Free Right Now

Published Oct 10, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

It is hard to believe that it has already been a year since the Nintendo Switch 2 launched, and with some incredible exclusive games already under its belt, not to mention the upcoming launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, it is safe to say that the latest Nintendo handheld has been a hit.

So, what if I told you that you could play the brand-new The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered on the Nintendo Switch 2 for absolutely free? Even if you have never owned it previously.

Launching earlier this month, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered offers exactly what it says on the tin: an enhanced version of 2015's The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, welcoming improved visuals and rendering, gameplay, UI and UX, accessibility, quality-of-life, and much more.

Since its launch, the remastered version of this hit RPG is already breaking records, and as well as launching on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and XBOX Series X/S as a free upgrade for those who already own a copy of the original title, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered also launched on the Nintendo Switch 2.

What we do know, is that for those who already own The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt on the Nintendo Switch, a free upgrade for the Nintendo Switch 2 will be available, much like on other platforms. However, as well as being possible courtesy of a digital download, it will also work with a physical cartridge.

As such, thanks to SwitchPlayed on YouTube, there is a way to play The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered on the Nintendo Switch 2 for free. As the Switch 2 only needs access to the cartridge once, you can simply borrow a friend's or even a copy from the library, and insert it into your handheld. Then, make sure that you have updated The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered to its latest version, Ver. 4.04d.

Once in game, head to the bottom of the main menu and the option 'AVAILABLE NOW ON NINTENDO SWITCH 2' should be available. Simply click on it and you are done. You now have access to The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered on the Nintendo Switch 2 for absolutely free, but as our YouTuber explains, it is probably best to do this quickly as there is no doubt that Nintendo will soon patch this out.

However, as the top comment on the YouTube video reads, "This won’t be patched. There’s no other way to do it if you want the people who have the physical cart to be able to upgrade, which you do. Same sort of deal for Skyrim and Hogwarts Legacy, you don’t need the cart."

So, it remains to be seen if this neat little trick will stick around, but what we do know, is that Nintendo Switch 2 fans are definitely the winners when it comes to the launch of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered.

Russell Crowe's R-Rated 'Exorcist' Replacement Is Officially Back on Streaming

Image via Sony Pictures Releasing

Published Oct 10, 2026, 5:40 AM EDT

Chris is a Senior News Writer for Collider. He can be found in an IMAX screen, with his eyes watering and his ears bleeding for his own pleasure. He joined the news team in 2022 and accidentally fell upwards into a senior position despite his best efforts.
For reasons unknown, he enjoys analyzing box office receipts, giant sharks, and has become known as the go-to man for all things Bosch, Mission: Impossible and Christopher Nolan in Collider's news division. Recently, he found himself yeehawing along to the Dutton saga on the Yellowstone Ranch.
He is proficient in sarcasm, wit, Photoshop and working unfeasibly long hours. Amongst his passions sit the likes of the history of the Walt Disney Company, the construction of theme parks, steam trains and binge-watching Gilmore Girls with a coffee that is just hot enough to scald him.
His obsession with the Apple TV+ series Silo is the subject of mockery within the Senior News channel, where his feelings about Taylor Sheridan's work are enough to make his fellow writers roll their eyes.

There are plenty of exorcism movies to choose from in October, but not many of them have Russell Crowe riding around Italy on a tiny Vespa while working directly for the Pope. That alone helped turn one relatively modest horror movie into a surprise theatrical hit — and eventually a franchise.

That movie is The Pope's Exorcist, and it has officially found a new streaming home on Prime Video just in time for Halloween. The 2023 supernatural horror movie made more than $77 million worldwide against a reported budget of around $18 million, which is a pretty healthy return for Crowe fighting demons. What's more, producer Jeff Katz soon announced a sequel would be on the way on social media, although that's gone quiet for the moment.

Katz also hinted at possible titles for the sequel, inspired by the naming style of the Planet of the Apes series. "I personally want to go Planet of the Apes with it so you would get stuff like 'Pray for the Pope's Exorcist' or 'Heaven Help the Pope's Exorcist' and the like," he said, while Crowe also recently discussed the potential expansion of the series. In an interview with The Six O'Clock Show, he mentioned the possibility of a trilogy.

"Well that's in discussion at the moment," Crowe explained. "The producers originally got the kick off from the studio not just for one sequel but for two. But there's been a change of studio heads at the moment, so that's going around in a few circles. But very definitely, man. We set that character up that you could take him out and put him into a lot of different circumstances." He also noted the extensive source material available, based on the life of Father Gabriele Amorth, who authored 12 books.

What Is Your Biggest Horror Nightmare?
Elm Street · Chucky · Scream · The Conjuring

Four horror franchises. Four completely different ways of scaring you. One waits until you fall asleep. One makes sure nobody believes you. One is already in your group of friends. And one is in the house with your family. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually watch horror, and find out which nightmare was built for you.

🧸Chucky(Child's Play)

📞Scream(Ghostface)

🕯️The Conjuring(The Warren Files)

FIND YOUR NIGHTMARE →

01

Which horror scene makes you cover your eyes?
Four classic images. One of them is worse than the others for you.

ASomebody falling asleep when they really should not.
BA toy that has moved, and nobody touched it.
CA phone ringing in an empty house.
DA child talking to somebody who is not there.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

You are home alone and you hear a noise. First thought?
Everybody has one. It arrives before you have decided anything.

AI am exhausted and my mind is playing tricks on me.
BSomething in this room is not where I left it.
CSomebody is in here with me.
DThis house has never felt entirely right.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Which horror movie rule would you break first?
Everybody thinks they would survive. Almost nobody actually does.

ANever fall asleep.
BNever leave it out of your sight.
CNever answer the phone.
DNever go down to the basement.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Something genuinely frightening happens. What do you do?
Not in a film. In your actual living room, tonight.

AConvince myself I imagined the whole thing.
BTell someone, and brace for them not believing me.
CWork out which person I know could be behind it.
DGet everybody in the house into one room.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How do you actually watch a horror film?
Be honest about this one. Nobody is checking.

AFine during. Wide awake at two in the morning.
BShouting at the screen that nobody is listening.
CCalling the twist out loud before it lands.
DThrough my fingers, holding on to something.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Somebody offers you serious money. Which do you still refuse?
The amount does not matter. There is one on this list you are not doing.

AFall asleep in a room I have never been in before.
BKeep an old doll on the shelf facing my bed.
CAnswer every unknown number that calls after midnight.
DSpend one night alone in a house with a history.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Which feeling stays with you a week after the film?
Good horror does not stop when the credits do.

ANot wanting to turn the bedroom light off.
BNot trusting one particular object in my house.
CLooking twice at people I have known for years.
DFeeling like something came home with me.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Something wakes you at 3am. What is the worst possibility?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your nightmare.

AThat I am still asleep, and it knows it.
BThat the thing nobody believed me about is here.
CThat somebody with a key is downstairs.
DThat something is in the doorway, watching us sleep.

REVEAL MY NIGHTMARE →

Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.

A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984

Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.

You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.

Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988

Chucky

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.

By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.

Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996

Scream

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.

Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.

The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013

The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

What Was 'The Pope's Exorcist' About?

Father Amorth, upon whom the movie is loosely based, was a significant figure within the Catholic Church. He served as the Chief Exorcist of the Vatican and claimed to have performed over 100,000 exorcisms during his career. However, Amorth also acknowledged that many of the cases he encountered were not demonic possessions but mental health issues. His fascinating life and work led him to found the International Association of Exorcists. His experiences have been documented in various books and were also featured in William Friedkin's 2017 documentary, The Devil and Father Amorth. The Pope's Exorcist draws heavily from Amorth's real case files, blending fact with cinematic fiction to tell its compelling story.

Stay tuned to Collider for updates on the sequel to The Pope's Exorcist.

Release Date

April 5, 2023

Runtime

103 Minutes

Director

Julius Avery

Writers

Evan Spiliotopoulos, Michael Petroni

Image via Warner Bros. Pictures

Chris is a Senior News Writer for Collider. He can be found in an IMAX screen, with his eyes watering and his ears bleeding for his own pleasure. He joined the news team in 2022 and accidentally fell upwards into a senior position despite his best efforts.
For reasons unknown, he enjoys analyzing box office receipts, giant sharks, and has become known as the go-to man for all things Bosch, Mission: Impossible and Christopher Nolan in Collider's news division. Recently, he found himself yeehawing along to the Dutton saga on the Yellowstone Ranch.
He is proficient in sarcasm, wit, Photoshop and working unfeasibly long hours. Amongst his passions sit the likes of the history of the Walt Disney Company, the construction of theme parks, steam trains and binge-watching Gilmore Girls with a coffee that is just hot enough to scald him.
His obsession with the Apple TV+ series Silo is the subject of mockery within the Senior News channel, where his feelings about Taylor Sheridan's work are enough to make his fellow writers roll their eyes.

Some sci-fi movies flop because they just don't hit audiences properly, perhaps because they go in to see one film and end up seeing a miserable Ryan Gosling wandering around a dreadful, dusty-yet-neon-soaked dystopia for almost three hours. This one made $259 million, lost money anyway, and then spent the next nine years being called one of the best science-fiction movies of the century. Funny how that works.

Blade Runner 2049, the sci-fi epic from Denis Villeneuve and producer Ridley Scott, has officially found a new streaming home on Prime Video. The sequel to Scott's 1982 classic arrives almost a decade after its theatrical release, and its reputation is far stronger than the box office returns it collected would have suggested.

Thirty years after the events of the first film, a new blade runner, LAPD Officer K, unearths a long-buried secret that has the potential to plunge what's left of society into chaos. K's discovery leads him on a quest to find Rick Deckard, a former LAPD blade runner who has been missing for 30 years.

Gosling (Drive) stars as K alongside Harrison Ford (Indiana Jones) as Deckard, Ana de Armas (Knives Out) as Joi, Sylvia Hoeks (See) as Luv, Robin Wright (House of Cards) as Lieutenant Joshi, Mackenzie Davis (Terminator: Dark Fate) as Mariette, Dave Bautista (Guardians of the Galaxy) as Sapper Morton, and Jared Leto (Dallas Buyers Club) as Niander Wallace.

How Good Is 'Blade Runner 2049?

Very. Blade Runner 2049 holds an 88% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, and Villeneuve somehow managed to make a sequel to one of the most respected sci-fi movies ever without embarrassing himself, which was hardly guaranteed. The box office was the problem. Blade Runner 2049 cost somewhere around $150 million before marketing and finished with roughly $259 million worldwide. Scott, never a man to miss a chance to fail to mince his words, offered a fairly simple explanation for why it struggled: “It's slow. It's long. Too long.”

He wasn't wrong about the runtime — the movie lasts 164 minutes — but that's also part of what makes it work. Villeneuve gives the world room to breathe, while cinematographer Roger Deakins finally won his first Academy Award after 13 previous nominations.

Blade Runner 2049 is streaming now on Prime Video.
