items.text:
The descent into autumn continues: this week I slept with an extra blanket on the bed. I'm not into swapping the duvet out for the winter tog yet, I'll be holding off on that until at least December, but the laying of the first blanket is a true marker of autumn's arrival.

Another change I was telling the team about to definitely rapt fascination was that I've brought the dehumidifier out to reduce condensation in the living room when drying washing. Not only that, I'm combining it with the fan I bought in summer to keep the air circulating. Reader, I don't mean to boast, but it dried two loads of washing including heavy ply towels overnight.

But enough about my successes, this is what the rest of the team are up to.

Edwin
This weekend I'll be checking out the demo for Ablahshikar, a turn-based ship-salvaging game with ASCII art and some extremely extra writing. As the developers put it: "Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." Ta to former RPS scribe and current Steam Hype editor Dominic Tarason for passing it on.

Mark
I've got another mystery game I'm slowly chipping away at. When I'm not on with that I might finally get around to checking out The Witcher 3's new coat of paint. I just need to double check I've not got any residue left over from a previous modded installation where I'd turned Gerry into a man-torsoed and horse-legged centaur, since that might cause the new version of the all-timer RPG to get a bit confused. I'm also due a return to Star Wars: Galactic Racer for a proper taste of its multiplayer now the podracing gates have opened to everyone.

Ollie
This weekend I'll be away from my... well, not my PC, because that's still borked. But my PC setup. Which is an important distinction, because for the time being I've been plugging my two monitors and all my peripherals into my laptop and playing on there, to varying degrees of success. But this weekend I'm travelling, so I've packed up said laptop - and also brought along my Steam Deck, my Steam Frame, and my Steam Controller. No, I'm not sponsored. I just don't know what I want to play or how I want to play it.

James
Wait, Ollie has a Steam Frame? At last, a second person I know who does. On a related note, there's a Titanfall 2 VR mod I've been meaning to try, and am finally free enough from review duties to make the time for it.

Jeremy
I'm playing an upcoming game that involves exploring a very large area, attacking things, and occasionally eating big pieces of chicken. You commentators who have been following my WAPs recently will figure it out.

Callum
Upon learning it was his one year anniversary at RPS, Callum announced he was departing for the sewers to "make good on the pact". We wish him good luck.

Julian
No doubt I will be hanging up more washing and testing this fan/dehumidifier system to check it wasn't just a fluke. But, if that doesn't take up all my time, I will also be playing some Dorfromantik. I've had my eye on it for a while but after talking to the Volatiles devs about it's tile placing mechanic I was convinced to finally buy it.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

Published Oct 10, 2026, 1:31 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

Airing from 2010 to 2022, The Walking Dead has been a constant companion of many of us growing up, with the hit post-apocalyptic horror show giving us 11 seasons and 177 episodes of blood, gore, heartache, and iconic moments. Despite the main coming to an end, the universe has most certainly not, with multiple spin-off shows airing since, including the currently airing The Walking Dead: Dead City and The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon.

However, there is no denying that nostalgia is a powerful emotion, and looking back at our original The Walking Dead cast as they first appeared back in season one is enough to trigger bittersweet memories. That being said, what if I told you that there was a way to experience the original cast once again?

Courtesy of The Walking Dead: Aftermath, fans can now head back to the very beginning after Rick Grimes awakes from his coma to see a world completely changed. As the official synopsis reads:

The dead walk. Society has fallen. Survival is all that remains.

Rick Grimes woke from a coma to find the world transformed. Cities abandoned. Families torn apart. The living forced to become something new just to survive. Step into the world of AMC’s The Walking Dead universe and begin your journey where it all started, in an action game shaped by the characters and stories fans know and love.

The Walking Dead: Aftermath is a mobile game for Android which will see you begin your journey on the outskirts of Atlanta and become the fearless leader of a fragile camp that is struggling to endure the ongoing apocalypse. With the constant threat of Walkers and the ever-dwindling supplies, it will be up to you to keep your people alive, and most importantly, help them thrive in the terrifying new world.

Perhaps most exciting is the news that you will get to take on the role of The Walking Dead's most iconic characters, such as Rick Grimes himself, as well as Daryl Dixon, Michonne, Glenn, and Maggie. With each survivor offering their own unique weapons and abilities, you will need to master precision, power, and survival instincts in order to make every encounter work in your favor.

Survival is not just about fighting the dead. It is about protecting the living.

Fans of survival games, roguelite progression, and action RPG gameplay will find a fast-paced experience built around skill, growth, and replayability.

The world has ended. The fight has just begun.

How long can you survive?

Now available on Android, The Walking Dead: Aftermath features iconic locations inspired by AMC's The Walking Dead, dangerous enemies both Walker and human, the ability to build and defend your camp, and of course, hordes of enemies which you will have to take down in order to keep your people safe.

With over one million downloads, it is safe to say that fans of The Walking Dead will not want to miss out on this hit mobile game, and become the ultimate post-apocalyptic survivor.

items.title: 35 English Loanwords That Come From the Japanese Language
items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer
items.summary: While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly
items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

8. Dashi　(だし)

No mention of washoku can exclude dashi, stock made from fish or kelp that is used as the base for many Japanese dishes. Dashi is commonly used in English to mean the same thing.

9. Katsu (curry or chicken katsu)　(かつ)

Katsu refers to cutlets of meat that are breaded using panko and deep-fried. The cutlets are usually pork or chicken. Katsu is served with a sauce or with curry. In fact, in some places overseas, katsu curry has become so popular that the term is used to mean all Japanese curry.

10. Panko　(パン粉)

You might have guessed this from the previous entry, but panko is breadcrumbs. They are commonly used in Japanese cooking and the product and the name have crossed over into English-speaking cultures.

The word panko is actually a combination of a loanword that didn’t come from English and the original Japanese word. “Pan” came from the Portuguese language, pao, and ko (粉) is a Japanese word that means “flour” or “dust”.

The biggest difference between panko and standard breadcrumbs is that panko is made from bread without crusts. Panko’s crustless white bread is coarsely ground into airy, large flakes that give fried foods a light, crunchy coating.

11. Amazake (甘酒)

Making the list of words of Japanese origin recently recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary, amazake is a sweet, fermented drink made from rice. Unlike sake, which is also made from rice, amazake is not alcoholic. It literally means sweet (ama) sake.

12. Manga (漫画)

These loanwords are used the same way in English as they are in Japanese. One distinction is that while manga means comics in general in Japan, the term typically means Japanese comics in English.

13. Anime (アニメ)

Probably the most popular loanword used all the time in English is アニメ (anime), which ironically comes from the word “animation” borrowed from English. But in English, “anime” specifically refers to Japanese animation even though in Japanese it refers to all animation. This term is a great example of words being traded back and forth between two languages.

14. Emoji　(絵文字)

Texting and instant messaging is just not the same without emoji, graphics that help express an emotion when words are just not enough. But the cute, yellow pictogram you’ve been using on your iPhone? The word came from the Japanese language. The kanji 絵 (え) means “picture” and 文字 (もじ) means “character” or “letter.” You might learn some new emoji from the Emojipedia online.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Sport and Martial Arts

Japanese martial arts are known the world over by their Japanese names. These are quite established loanwords, and the sports themselves continue to gain devotees.

15. Judo　(柔道)

Japanese martial arts are well-known throughout the English-speaking world, by their Japanese names. Judo, a defensive martial art, is no exception. The term originates from soft, gentle (柔; juu) and way, road (道; do). Judo is an Olympic event, and practitioners are usually called judoka (柔道家).

When you’re saying the word “judo” in Japanese, remember to elongate the first syllable: Ju-u-dou. In English, however, you can shorten it.

16. Jujutsu　(柔術)

Precursor to judo, this is also a Japanese unarmed martial art. The first part of the term, juu means gentle, just like in judo and the jutsu (術) means skill or art. There are variant spellings in English, including jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. It is also the origin of the name of the famous martial art, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

However, historical evidence shows that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ) comes from Judo, but at the time Judo was still being called “Ju-Jutsu,” which is why BJJ has its name today rather than “Brazilian Judo.”

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).

18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”

19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts

From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.

20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).

21. Noh　(能)

In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.

22. Tanka　(短歌)

A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.

23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.

Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.

23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.

Other Japanese Loanwords We Use in English

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.

25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.

26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.

27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.

28. Zen　(善)

This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.

29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.

30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.

31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.

32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.

Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.

33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.

34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.

35. Shinkansen (新幹線)

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Japan’s efficient transportation system, particularly the bullet train, has become such an image of the nation that shinkansen is now widely known in English. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”

Conclusion:

You might be surprised how many words the English language adopts from Japanese alone. You’ve no doubt been using many of them and as the English language continues to borrow words from Japanese, you’ll end up using even more Japanese, in English. The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. items.text:
If you have started learning Japanese or thinking about doing it soon, you might ask yourself: How long does it take to learn Japanese? It’s an honest question, and probably the most important. Between people’s fascination with Japanese culture and the desire to live in Japan, Japanese has become one of the most popular languages to learn – but also the hardest, too.

The answer to this question is, “it depends”. Understandably, no one likes to hear that — but it’s an honest answer because there’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to how long it takes to learn Japanese. On a complete beginner-to-advanced scale, it takes around 180 to 1,2000 hours to learn Japanese. In reality, people with no prior kanji knowledge often take more time to learn Japanese thanthose who have.

In this response, we’ll explore the factors that can affect how long it takes to learn Japanese and provide estimates of how long it may take a beginner to become proficient.

Defining Fluency in Japanese Language Learning

To the majority, language fluency is a spectrum. You can talk to your Japanese friends in casual Japanese and call it fluent. You might think that to be one means being able to lead a meeting with your coworkers in full keigo.

A good rule of thumb is if you find yourself constantly translating between Japanese and your own native language and forming sentences quickly, you’d be hard-pressed to describe yourself as fluent. In its academic definition, made by Dr. Paul Nation and Asuza Yamamoto, fluency is ‘being able to receive and produce language at a reasonable rate’. You should ask yourself, “Am I at ease when I speak Japanese? Do I get constantly worried about the next question from my partner?”

On the other hand, this number begs the question: Can I call myself fluent if I can watch anime without subtitles? Can I talk to my Japanese friends without fillers like eto or ano? Or write a foolproof business email to your Japanese boss?

Remember that there’s more to communication than speaking and listening! Japanese language fluency also includes four aspects: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. You may be excellent at conversing in Japanese, but barely able to write a single kanji.

So depending on how you define fluency, you might get to that point faster or slower! And don’t worry: we’ve broken down the study hours based on your goal and the desired level below.

How Long Does it Take to Learn Japanese Based on Your Goal?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. This is probably a fairer assessment than saying it takes 2 years to speak Japanese. The more hours you put into practicing Japanese in a day or stay consistent throughout the week, the faster you’ll learn.

Ultimately, achieving a high level in Japanese takes time, as with other languages. A lot of people who live in Japan and studied the language for years might still say they have a long way to go, so you can’t expect instant results in a matter of weeks.

As a reference, we’ve broken down how long it takes to learn Japanese based on what you’re using the language for. Depending on your goal, you might want to focus on one language aspect (like speaking) more than the other.

GoalHow you’ll use JapaneseStudy Hours

TravelAsk for directions, order food, and make basic greetings.7 – 30 days

Make friendsDaily conversations, expressing thoughts and opinions, holding natural conversations in a wider range of circumstances.900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

Work part-time job in JapanSpeak basic keigo to customers, interact with Japanese coworkers900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

Get a job in JapanTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination) and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, and make a presentation2,000 – 4,000 study hours (2 years)

Go to universityTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination, and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, make a presentationUse keigo (Japanese honorifics), business Japanese, manners, and cultural awareness, JLPT (N2 or N1)

How Many Hours a Day Should You Study Japanese

You might notice we’ve been using “study hours” instead of exact days or months, which can be frustrating if you want a straightforward answer on how long it takes to learn Japanese.

Days and months can vary in length and can be influenced by external factors, such as holidays or personal schedules, making it difficult to accurately track progress. There are people who might study 30 minutes a day. Some dedicate 3 hours a day, while a few people spend 6-7 hours studying full-time. This isn’t the best standardized unit of time.

Be warned: you are about to read the most groan-worthy Japanese dad jokes ever! 親父ギャグ (Oyaji gyagu), literally meaning “old man gags,” is the Japanese equivalent of “dad jokes.” They are characterized by cheesy puns, or ダジャレ in Japanese. Similar to English, Japanese puns are built on homophones, or words that sound the same but have different meanings.

Dad jokes are just as cheesy in Japanese as they are in any language, but they are a great way to learn about Japanese culture and humor while practicing informal sentence structures. Japanese dad jokes can help with picking up natural language through their use of non-literal, figurative language.

What Are Japanese Dad Jokes or 親父ギャグ (Oyaji Gagu)?

Most Japanese dad jokes use homophones, a fancy grammatical term for when two different words, with different meanings, sound very similar. Since the Japanese language only has a limited number of unique syllables to build words from, homophones end up being very common, and it’s quite easy to make corny jokes out of them. This is the basis of many dad jokes and ダジャレ in general.

Onomatopoeia, or the written form of action sounds, are abundant in the Japanese language, so they are another common component of dad jokes.

1. このステーキはすてき！(kono suteeki wa suteki!)

Romaji: Kono suteeki wa suteki!
Meaning: The steak is wonderful!
Joke Explanation:
Steak → ステーキ (suteeki)
Wonderful → ステキ (suteki)

A classic, simple homophone that relies on nearly identical sounds, and the best part is that it only requires JLPT N5 knowledge to understand! ステーキ, meaning beef steak, a dad’s favorite food, is said quickly in a shortened form to sound just like ステキ, which means lovely or wonderful.

ステキな isn’t a very natural way to describe delicious food, so the intentional word choice elicits the inevitable groan. For natural, casual ways to describe food, you can combine the prefixes めちゃ or マジで, meaning very, with おいしい or うまい, meaning tasty.

2. 美味すぎて、馬になった。(umasugite, uma ni natta.)

Romaji: umasugite, uma ni natta
Meaning: It was so delicious I turned into a horse.
Joke Explanation:
Delicious → 美味い (umai)
Horse → 馬 (uma)

The pun comes from the similar sounds of 馬 (uma), meaning horse, and 美味い (umai), meaning “delicious.” The joke also incorporates a bit of N4 grammar: the suffix すぎる (sugiru), which means “too much.”

For example, if you want to emphasize how cold it is outside on the first day of winter, you may say さむすぎる instead of just さむい. The て form lets you connect clauses fluidly, showing cause and relation or the order of events. 馬 is the corresponding second homophone, followed by なった, the past tense form of なる, meaning to become.

3. 土管の中でドッカーン (Dokan no naka de dokkaan.)

Romaji: Dokan no naka de dokkaan.
Meaning: Kaboom inside the clay pipe.
Joke Explanation:
Clay Pipe → 土管 (dokan)
Kaboom →ドッカーン

This one is a combination effect of onomatopoeia with homophones. This joke that relies on more advanced kanji & vocabulary (around N1 level), using the very particular word for clay / earthen pipe土管 to sound like the onomatopoeia ドッカーン. A very simple N5 grammatical structure using の中で as a prepositional phrase, denoting where the kaboom took place. What makes this joke a bit more difficult is the advanced-level vocab 土管, which you will probably never encounter unless you read construction signs.

4. 餃子を食べて、仰天！(gyoza o tabete, gyoten!)

Romaji: gyoza o tabete, gyoten!
Meaning: I ate the gyoza and was amazed!
Joke Explanation:
Gyoza → 餃子
Amazed → 仰天 (gyoten)

This dad joke is a simple homophone that rhymes the popular Japanese dumplings, gyoza, with the expression of amazement, gyoten. Once again, we see the て- form grammar connecting the two clauses.

To read, this joke relies on more niche N3-level kanji knowledge. While 餃子 may be easier for foodies to recognize, 仰天 is quite advanced for learners. Still, this dad joke is easy to remember for your next visit to a Chinese restaurant!

5. チーターが池におっこちーたー. (Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.)

Romaji: Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.
Meaning: The cheetah fell into the pond.
Joke Explanation:
Cheetah → チーター
Fall down → 落っこちる (okkochiru)

This is more of an N2-level joke because the dramatized, colloquial form of 落ちる used in this joke isn’t commonly learned or taught early on. The rest of the rhyme uses easier vocabulary and grammar. We see が used once again as a subject particle, describing what the cheetah is doing. Combining this with the kanji for pond, 池, and using に as a preposition for the direction of the cheetah sets us up for the punchline.

The informal past tense of “to fall down” sounds just like the katakana word for cheetah, if dragged out, completing our homophonic dad joke. Once again, 落っこちる is more of a spoken, dramatized version of 落ちる

6. イルカはいるか？(iruka wa iruka?)

Romaji: Iruka wa iruka
Meaning: Are there any dolphins?
Joke Explanation:
Dolphin → イルカ
there is (living subject) → いる

This joke is as easy and cheesy as it gets. イルカ is written in katakana mainly because the kanji is hard to read, so it’s more convenient and accessible. は is used as our subject particle, as the dolphins are the subject of our silly question. いる, the word for “there is” when referring to animate subjects, is given the informal suffix か to turn it into a question. Maybe use this dad joke when you visit the Sumida Aquarium near Tokyo Skytree to test some reactions.

7. 車で、来るまで待つ。(kuruma de, kuru made matsu.)

Romaji: kuruma de kuru made matsu
Meaning: I will wait until they come by car.
Joke Explanation:
Car → 車 (kuruma)
Come → 来る (kuru)
Until → まで

Great for beginners to stretch their minds, this one uses a somewhat clever homophone, relying on the connection between 来る and まで to form the punchline. A phonetic mirror, if executed perfectly, 来るまで should sound just like 車 being enunciated poorly. 待つ is an N5-level vocabulary word meaning to wait. まで has several grammatical uses, but here it signifies waiting for the preceding action to occur.

8. 歯科医師が司会した。(shikaishi ga shikaishita)

Romaji: shikaishi ga shikaishita
Meaning: The dentist moderated the meeting
Joke Explanation:
Dentist → 歯科医師 (shikaishi)
Moderated → 司会する (shikai suru)

Because of the vocabulary it uses, this joke might be around N2 level. It’s structurally similar to the homophone examples we explained earlier, but it requires advanced kanji & vocab knowledge. This joke rests on the past tense of 司会する (shikaisuru), which is 司会した (shikaishita), meaning “led” or “moderated”.

To pull this dad joke off, you must pronounce 司会した (shikaishita) to sound exactly like 歯科医師 (shikaishita), which takes some over-enunciation of the し in した.

9. 電話に出んわ (Denwa ni denwa)

Romaji: denwa ni denwa
Meaning: I won’t answer the phone.
Explanation:
Phone → 電話 (denwa)
Answer → 出る (deru)

While the grammar and vocabulary are quite simple, the use of a different Japanese dialect could confuse beginners. This dad joke uses the Kansai dialect, which you may hear in Osaka or around Kyoto. The punchline of the joke takes the standard phrase 電話に出ない, dropping ない (nai) and adding ん (n), a shortened negative form, and the Kansai suffix わ, used to express emphasis. Now, 出ない sounds like denwa, similar to the word for “phone” or “call.”

In English, depending on where you learned to speak, we all say things a bit differently. The same applies to Japan, where different regions have their own way of saying things. One of the main alternatives to standard Japanese is the rough-sounding Kansai dialect.

10. 私はニューヨークで入浴した。(watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuuyokushita.)

Romaji: Watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuyokushita
Meaning: I took a bath in New York.
Explanation:
Bathing (formal) → 入浴 (nyuuyoku)
New York → ニューヨーク

Although this joke is grammatically simple, the term 入浴 (nyuuyoku) is very formal and uses old kanji that you will likely only see at an onsen. If you stretch out 入浴 (nyuuyoku), it sounds like how you would pronounce New York in katakana: ニューヨーク (nyuuyooku).

Combining these two homophones with the particle で, which denotes the location of the action, means the bath was taken in New York. Onsen are where you might see this kanji used seriously, for example: 入浴時間 (nyuuyoku jikan), meaning bathing hours.

How to Make Your Own Japanese Dad Jokes

Since these jokes are great practice for your Japanese skills no matter your level, consider playing around and writing your own. Here are a few easy steps to get you started.


Pay attention to homophones. Japanese’s limited number of unique syllables naturally creates many homophones.

Use simple grammar structures. These jokes don’t require difficult grammar, so don’t be afraid to form sentences informally.

Use what you know. This is the best way to master a language; using what you have learned in your own way will lead to a strong acquisition of Japanese.


Conclusion: Dad Jokes are Great for Practicing Japanese!

Once you get the hang of these puns, it is fun to use the vocab and grammar that you are familiar with to construct your own. This is a very basic one:

Salmon roe → いくら
How much? → いくら
いくらはいくら？
How much is the salmon roe?

Expressing your sense of humor is a huge part of language learning and speaking Japanese more naturally! Jokes aren’t only fun; they can help you remember more words and express yourself more freely without sticking to rigid, literal definitions!

Sharing a laugh may be one of the best ways to practice Japanese!

The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.title: The Best New Restaurants in Queens
items.summary: Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee
items.text:
Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee Astoria banquet hall, which opened in May. Amid business conventions, there’s marvelous seolleongtang: thick, white, and almost creamy from all the collagen that’s seeped out from hours of simmering beef bones. It comes with the customary fixings of scallions, sea salt, and pepper so everyone can season it to their liking. Tender beef also appears in the suyuk (boiled beef slices with dips) and what the restaurant calls lasagna dumplings: squares of dumpling stuffing with the wrapper on the top and bottom.

After a decades-long hustle, Burmese Bites chef and owner Myo Lin Thway has finally opened the full-service restaurant of his dreams. The former buffet-style Point Brazil in Astoria has transformed into a cool, bustling space with quick, kind service. All the bestsellers from Thway’s days at street festivals, Queens Night Market, and Queens Center Mall now rest in beautiful, colorful ceramics and thatched wood plateware. The must-orders: the assorted palatas like the chicken curry that kickstarted the business; tea leaf salad; ohno kauswe (coconut chicken noodle soup); mohinga (ground fish noodle soup); and crispy eel chile fries.

Xiaozhan is a fantastic rice noodle soup spot with a sauce bar in Flushing, which opened in May. All ten noodle soups are served in mini clay pots with bundles of slippery, slurpy, bouncy rice noodles; vegetables; and protein options such as fish, beef, shrimp, and chicken. The soup bases vary from mushrooms to assorted chile preparations (charred, pickled, oil), but the passionfruit stands out. It has a lovely balance of robust flavors — sour, spicy, savory — brightened up with passion fruit and lemon. And if you want more spiciness or umami, head to the sauce bar. The space is tiny, and wait times can exceed an hour, so go during off-peak hours.

Northwestern Queens can now grab some good Nigerian jollof and suya with the opening of the D.C.-based takeout chain Disbe Good, which opened inside the Sunnyside Eats ghost kitchen in May. The jollof is fluffy, tomato-based, and subtly spicy. But the charcoal-grilled smokiness of the suya is loud and proud — whether you opt for the beef, chicken, or lamb. And all the meats are halal. Every order comes with an extra helping of yaji, their quality suya spice blend of peanut, smoked paprika, and chile pepper, so you can use any leftovers for your own home cooking.

Woodside has gained a thoughtful restaurant that pushes the boundaries of typical Japanese American restaurants in New York with Tomoni, which opened in April. Lunch sets include common premium offerings like wagyu or eel donburi, but the perfectly cooked protein portions are generous. But Tomoni also offers misozuke cream cheese, which has been marinated in miso for two days and served with nori and wasabi; it’s delightful: nutty and slightly sweet. There’s also the raw octopus (a small bowl of shredded octopus in a slightly vinegary seasoning) and natto (the sticky, stringy fermented soybeans usually eaten at home). It’s served with rice, sauce, a raw pasteurized egg, a couple of slices of grilled eel, tamagoyaki, and miso soup.

What looks small and divey from the front opens up into a large Chinese banquet hall-type space. Peruse a massive menu of Cantonese classics that had been sorely missing in NYC’s newest Chinatown. Fresh lobster is coated in a garlicky brown sauce. Fried whole anchovies are tossed in salt and pepper. Stellar snow pea sprouts get braised in a light savory broth, topped with fried shrimp, and served in a cast iron pot. Head over for weekday lunch specials ($14-17) on entrees like beef stew with radish and chicken with cashews — all served with soup and rice.

A new Uzbek restaurant has been doling out traditional dishes in Rego Park since April. Registan Plov Center lives up to its name with a plov that’s freshly made daily in the mornings. It’s a dome of rice, chickpeas, lamb, and cubed carrots with pops of sweetness from raisins — all tantalizingly slicked with lamb fat. Get the grilled lamb ribs, too. It’s served on a mountain of sliced lemon and tomato, topped with potato chips and a flourish of sliced onions. Wash it all down with kompot, a light seasonal fruit juice; it’s mixed berries for summer.

On the weekends, all the Forest Hills families are at the massive new location of Turkish American chain Zara, which opened in May. Of the many highlights, the huge complimentary balloon bread — that’s the length of an arm and puffed up straight out of the open-flame oven — might be the greatest. Rip into it and dip into spreads like labneh, hummus, and babaganoush. Or wrap it around grilled kababs, short ribs, and steaks. Leave room for desserts. The tas kadayif is made fresh to order: pan-fried pastry stuffed with walnuts and honey, which is served with vanilla ice cream.

It comes with the customary fixings of scallions, sea salt, and pepper so everyone can season it to their liking. Tender beef also appears in the suyuk (boiled beef slices with dips) and what the restaurant calls lasagna dumplings: squares of dumpling stuffing with the wrapper on the top and bottom.

blocks.x: After a decades-long hustle, Burmese Bites chef and owner Myo Lin Thway has finally opened the full-service restaurant of his dreams. The former buffet-style Point Brazil in Astoria has transformed into a cool, bustling space with quick, kind service. All the bestsellers from Thway’s days at street festivals, Queens Night Market, and Queens Center Mall now rest in beautiful, colorful ceramics and thatched wood plateware. The must-orders: the assorted palatas like the chicken curry that kickstarted the business; tea leaf salad; ohno kauswe (coconut chicken noodle soup); mohinga (ground fish noodle soup); and crispy eel chile fries.

Xiaozhan is a fantastic rice noodle soup spot with a sauce bar in Flushing, which opened in May. All ten noodle soups are served in mini clay pots with bundles of slippery, slurpy, bouncy rice noodles; vegetables; and protein options such as fish, beef, shrimp, and chicken. The soup bases vary from mushrooms to assorted chile preparations (charred, pickled, oil), but the passionfruit stands out. It has a lovely balance of robust flavors — sour, spicy, savory — brightened up with passion fruit and lemon. And if you want more spiciness or umami, head to the sauce bar. The space is tiny, and wait times can exceed an hour, so go during off-peak hours.

Northwestern Queens can now grab some good Nigerian jollof and suya with the opening of the D.C.-based takeout chain Disbe Good, which opened inside the Sunnyside Eats ghost kitchen in May. The jollof is fluffy, tomato-based, and subtly spicy. But the charcoal-grilled smokiness of the suya is loud and proud — whether you opt for the beef, chicken, or lamb. And all the meats are halal. Every order comes with an extra helping of yaji, their quality suya spice blend of peanut, smoked paprika, and chile pepper, so you can use any leftovers for your own home cooking.

Woodside has gained a thoughtful restaurant that pushes the boundaries of typical Japanese American restaurants in New York with Tomoni, which opened in April. Lunch sets include common premium offerings like wagyu or eel donburi, but the perfectly cooked protein portions are generous. But Tomoni also offers misozuke cream cheese, which has been marinated in miso for two days and served with nori and wasabi; it’s delightful: nutty and slightly sweet. There’s also the raw octopus (a small bowl of shredded octopus in a slightly vinegary seasoning) and natto (the sticky, stringy fermented soybeans usually eaten at home). It’s served with rice, sauce, a raw pasteurized egg, a couple of slices of grilled eel, tamagoyaki, and miso soup.

Stellar snow pea sprouts get braised in a light savory broth, topped with fried shrimp, and served in a cast iron pot. Head over for weekday lunch specials ($14-17) on entrees like beef stew with radish and chicken with cashews — all served with soup and rice.

blocks.x: A new Uzbek restaurant has been doling out traditional dishes in Rego Park since April. Registan Plov Center lives up to its name with a plov that’s freshly made daily in the mornings. It’s a dome of rice, chickpeas, lamb, and cubed carrots with pops of sweetness from raisins — all tantalizingly slicked with lamb fat. Get the grilled lamb ribs, too. It’s served on a mountain of sliced lemon and tomato, topped with potato chips and a flourish of sliced onions. Wash it all down with kompot, a light seasonal fruit juice; it’s mixed berries for summer.

blocks.x: On the weekends, all the Forest Hills families are at the massive new location of Turkish American chain Zara, which opened in May. Of the many highlights, the huge complimentary balloon bread — that’s the length of an arm and puffed up straight out of the open-flame oven — might be the greatest. Rip into it and dip into spreads like labneh, hummus, and babaganoush. Or wrap it around grilled kababs, short ribs, and steaks. Leave room for desserts. The tas kadayif is made fresh to order: pan-fried pastry stuffed with walnuts and honey, which is served with vanilla ice cream.
